I would keep my farm simple and steady this year: I would do the usual winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. Around Quzhou, that is the main system, and it fits our weather and water pattern well: winter and spring are dry, so wheat needs irrigation, while most of our rain comes in summer, which suits maize. Quzhou is a typical North China Plain county with about 500 to 560 mm annual rainfall, and more than 80% of fields are in wheat-maize rotation, so I would stay with the crop pair I know best instead of spreading myself into cotton or vegetables. I’m basing that on Quzhou-specific and North China Plain sources here: [PMC survey on Quzhou crops](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10964062/), [Scientific Reports on Quzhou system](https://www.nature.com/articles/srep41587), [Quzhou climate/resource study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959652614000304).

Because I am 47 and only have primary schooling, I would not chase a complicated planting structure. I would put all my land into one wheat-maize double crop and manage it with straightforward machinery service, moderate fertilizer, and careful irrigation for wheat. I would use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed, plough or rotary-till before wheat, then no-till or direct sow maize right after wheat harvest to save time and moisture. I would keep fertilizer at a moderate level instead of pushing too hard, because wheat here can easily become too dependent on water and nitrogen, and I would rather aim for a stable yield than gamble on a very high one.
